parent.name: French Defense
parent.overview: Black plays ...e6 and ...d5, accepting a pawn chain and a space deficit in return for a sound position, and then hits White's pawn centre at its base with ...c5. The fight is over the dark squares d4 and e5. Black's problem piece is the light-squared bishop on c8, hemmed in by the e6 pawn; Black solves it by exchanging it or rerouting it (...b6 and ...Ba6, or ...Bd7 with ...Bb5/a4). White typically uses extra space for a kingside attack (f4-f5, and in the Advance the g4/h4 ideas) or expands on the queenside with a3-b4. Play is slower and manoeuvring, with a lot of pawn-break play. It has a reputation for solidity but a cramped early game for Black. The Winawer (3.Nc3 Bb4) is the sharpest branch, the Advance is the main fight in a locked centre, and the Tarrasch, Classical and Exchange are quieter. The root is one position after 1...e6 2.d4 d5; the structures differ strongly by branch.

parent.name: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bb5 a6 4. Ba4 Nf6 5. O-O
parent.overview: 3...a6 is the main road of the Ruy Lopez (roughly two thirds to 90 per cent of Ruy games per the sources). It asks White's bishop an immediate question: Bxc6 (Exchange) or the retreat 4.Ba4, after which Black can play ...b5 to kick the bishop again. The main line is the Closed Ruy (5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 d6 8.c3 O-O 9.h3), a locked, slow centre where White builds the c3-d4 pawn duo and reroutes the knight Nb1-d2-f1-g3, and Black seeks queenside counterplay with ...c5/...c4 or ...Bb7 and ...Re8/...Bf8. Alternatives at move five or later include the Open Variation (5...Nxe4), the Arkhangelsk (5...b5), and Marshall Attack (8...d5), with Anti-Marshall systems used by White to dodge it. Play is typically slow positional manoeuvring (the 'Spanish torture': a small White edge pressed for forty moves) with very deep theory. It has been a main weapon of nearly every world champion.

parent.name: Owen Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...b6 to fianchetto the queen's bishop on b7 and attack e4 from a distance, letting White take the centre with 2.d4 and then undermining it with ...e6, ...Nf6, ...Bb4 and the breaks ...c5 or ...d5. The main line is 2.d4 Bb7 3.Bd3 e6 4.Nf3 c5 5.c3, with 3.Nc3 (French-like) and 3.Nf3 also played. Black's kingside is a little loose and White is described as getting a space advantage and, with sensible play, a slight edge (Bauer) or around 60% wins in practice. Theory calls it slightly unsound but not refuted; it is rare at top level in classical play, although Carlsen, Nakamura and Firouzja have used it in online blitz. The 3...f5 Matovinsky Gambit is described as suicidal by Bauer.

parent.name: Dutch Defense
parent.overview: Black answers 1.d4 with 1...f5, fighting for e4 and avoiding symmetrical play, at the cost of weakening the kingside (the e8-h5 diagonal) and the e6 square. Three set-ups dominate: the Leningrad (...g6, ...Bg7, KID-style, with ...e5 or ...Ne4 and kingside play), the Stonewall (...e6, ...d5, ...c6 with a knight on e4 and a bad light-squared bishop) and the Classical (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...e5). White usually fianchettoes with g3/Bg2 and c4 and prepares e4 or queenside expansion, or sidesteps theory with the Staunton Gambit (2.e4), Hopton or Korchnoi Attack (h3 and g4). Sources agree it is sound but double-edged, unbalancing and theoretical, played occasionally by Carlsen, Nakamura and Nepomniachtchi but never a main defence to 1.d4.

parent.name: Center Game
parent.overview: White strikes the centre at once: 2.d4 exd4 3.Qxd4 regains the pawn and opens the game, at the cost of an early queen that Black hits with 3...Nc6. The queen goes to e3 (Paulsen's Attack, 4.Qe3), and White develops quickly with Nc3, Bd2, Bc4 or Be2, castles queenside and aims the queen and the semi-open d-file at g7 and the kingside, or pushes the h-pawn. Black has calm, sound set-ups (4...Nf6, 4...Be7 preparing ...d5, 4...g6, 4...Bb4+) and equalises with accurate play. Opposite-side castling can turn it into a race. Instead of 3.Qxd4, White can play 3.c3 (Danish Gambit), which is a separate gambit branch.

parent.name: Nimzowitsch Defense
parent.overview: Black develops a knight on move one and invites White to build a centre, planning to undermine it with timely pieces and pawn breaks (...d5, ...e5 or ...e6). The most common reply to 2.d4 is 2...d5 with 3.exd5 Qxd5 (Scandinavian-type), 3.e5 Bf5 (French-Advance-like with a freed bishop) or the 3.Nc3 dxe4 4.d5 Ne5 line, which is French-like in structure. Alternatively Black plays 2...e5 (Kennedy Variation), which can transpose to the Scotch, or 2...e6/2...g6 (Franco-Hiva, Pirc connection) with flexible set-ups. Kasparov and Keene wrote it has never been fully accepted as dependable, but sources agree it is far from refuted; players choose it to escape preparation and play non-standard but often French/Scandinavian-like middlegames. Roughly 2% of games per Chessable.

parent.name: Pirc Defense
parent.overview: Black plays 1...d6 and, after 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3, ...g6 and ...Bg7, letting White build the broad e4-d4 centre and then undermining it from the flanks with ...c5 or ...e5 (hypermodern: the bigger White's centre, the bigger the target). The root is a crossroads: 1...d6 can transpose to the Philidor (3...e5 or ...c6) or to the Modern. White's replies run from sharp (Austrian Attack 4.f4, 150 Attack 4.Be3 with Qd2, Bh6 and h4-h5, Byrne 4.Bg5, Bayonet h4) to unhurried (Classical 4.Nf3 with Be2 and castling, fianchetto). Typical play is imbalanced: White gets space and often a kingside attack, Black gets a solid fianchettoed king and counterplay on the queenside and with central breaks. It is sound but has a reputation for giving White chances; Kasparov doubted it for the top level (s1), though Caruana, Anand and Grischuk have used it (s2).

parent.name: Indian Defense: Anti-Nimzo-Indian
parent.overview: After 3.Nf3 White declines to allow the Nimzo-Indian pin (3.Nc3 Bb4) and leaves the structure open until Black reveals it. Black's reply decides the game: 3...d5 transposes to the Queen's Gambit Declined or the Catalan (the most popular, 40.2 percent at lower ratings and 43.4 percent at 2500), 3...b6 is the Queen's Indian, 3...Bb4+ the Bogo-Indian, and 3...c5 leads to Benoni-style structures (or the Blumenfeld Gambit). Chessiverse calls the move 'slightly more restrained' than 3.Nc3, offering numerous paths to a quiet, positional edge, and a flexible move order rather than a fixed system. Posters on the Chess.com forum point out that 3.Nf3 does not entirely avoid the Nimzo, since 3...Bb4+ 4.Nc3 reaches the Three Knights Nimzo, and that the consensus is that no black reply is worse than equal. White's edge shrinks as ratings rise.

parent.name: Hungarian Opening
parent.overview: White plays 1.g3 to fianchetto the king's bishop to g2 and hit the long diagonal, deferring any central commitment (s1, s3). It is a flank opening that usually transposes: into the King's Indian Attack (Nf3, d3, O-O, then e4), the Catalan, the Réti or the English, depending on Black's set-up (s1, s3, s4). Black can happily occupy the centre with ...d5 or ...e5, or choose Sicilian, Caro-Kann or King's Indian-style set-ups (s2, s3). Positions are usually closed or flexible, with long-term strategic play rather than early tactics (s1, s3). Engines and statistics find it essentially equal, with White at most slightly more comfortable (s3, s4). Theory is minimal: it is closer to a move order than a distinct variation (s2).

parent.name: Petrov's Defense
parent.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Nxe5 d6 4. Nf3 Nxe4
parent.overview: Black answers 2.Nf3 by counter-attacking e4 rather than defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 Nxe4 5.d4 d5 6.Bd3 both sides have lost an e-pawn and the structure is symmetrical, with the e-file the main open line. Black's aim is to equalise by quick development and piece trades; White tries to turn a small lead in development or slightly freer play into pressure, often castling and using the e-file or a queenside castling and pawn storm. The 3.d4 Steinitz line (3...Nxe4 4.Bd3 d5 5.Nxe5 Nd7) and 3.Nc3 (Four Knights transposition) or 3.d3 sidelines give quieter or more varied structures. The main lines are widely played at the top and are known as drawish, though some lines hold real attacking chances for both sides.
